title: THE VERSE THAT OFFENDS THE PART OF YOU THAT STILL WANTS TO DESERVE GRACE
paragraphs:
THE VERSE THAT OFFENDS THE PART OF YOU THAT STILL WANTS TO DESERVE GRACE
Why “The Last Will Be First” Is So Uncomfortable—and Why Jesus Told a Story That Exposes What Happens When Grace Is Given to Someone We Think Deserves Less Than Us
There is a sentence Jesus spoke that sounds beautiful...
until God applies it to somebody you do not think deserves what you received.
Then suddenly it becomes uncomfortable.
Painfully uncomfortable.
Because most of us love grace when we are the ones crawling toward it.
We love mercy when our own past is being discussed.
We love forgiveness when our name is attached to the scandal.
We love second chances when we are the ones who ruined the first one.
But watch what happens inside the human heart when Jesus gives astonishing mercy to somebody else.
Somebody who wasted years you spent serving.
Somebody who destroyed things you protected.
Somebody who lived recklessly while you tried to remain faithful.
Somebody who showed up late.
Somebody whose testimony contains chapters that would make church people whisper.
Somebody who seems to walk into the vineyard at the eleventh hour...
and somehow still leaves carrying the generosity of the Master.
That is where grace stops being merely comforting.
That is where grace becomes confrontational.
And Jesus knew it.
He said:
“Πολλοὶ δὲ ἔσονται πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.”
Polloi de esontai prōtoi eschatoi kai eschatoi prōtoi.
“But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
Matthew 19:30
The words matter.
Prōtoi—πρῶτοι—means “first,” “foremost,” those at the front.
Eschatoi—ἔσχατοι—means “last,” those at the far end.
Jesus takes the categories human beings instinctively understand...
first.
last.
ahead.
behind.
important.
unimportant.
deserving.
undeserving.
And turns them upside down.
But we should not rip that sentence out of its context and turn it into a motivational slogan about underdogs eventually becoming successful.
Jesus was saying something far more dangerous to human pride.
Just before these words, a rich young man had approached Jesus.
He possessed much.
Yet when Jesus confronted the place where his possessions possessed him, the man walked away sorrowful.
The disciples were stunned by what followed.
Jesus spoke about how difficult it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven.
They asked:
“Who then can be saved?”
And Jesus gave the answer that stands over every genuine conversion:
“With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
Then Peter spoke.
And Peter's question is more relatable than most Christians would like to admit.
“We have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?”
In other words...
Lord, we stayed.
Lord, we sacrificed.
Lord, we followed.
Lord, we gave things up.
So...
what do we get?
Jesus did not condemn Peter for following Him. In fact, He promised extraordinary reward to those who had sacrificed for His name.
But then He added the warning:
Many who are first will be last.
And the last first.
Then Matthew moves directly into one of Jesus' most unsettling parables.
A landowner goes out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.
Some begin early.
Others come later.
More are hired later still.
Then near the end of the working day, the landowner finds others standing there.
They have barely any daylight left.
They enter the vineyard late.
And when evening comes, payment begins.
But something strange happens.
The last are called first.
And those who worked only a short time receive a denarius.
Imagine standing in that line if you had worked since morning.
You see the latecomer receive a full day's wage.
Your exhausted mind immediately starts calculating.
“If he got that much...
imagine what I'm getting.”
Then your turn comes.
And you receive...
a denarius.
The same amount originally agreed upon.
Suddenly what had been perfectly fair minutes earlier feels insulting.
Why?
Nothing was taken from the early workers.
The landowner kept his agreement.
Their anger was awakened not because they received injustice...
but because somebody else received generosity.
There it is.
The wound beneath the wound.
The scandal beneath the scandal.
Sometimes we are not angry because God has been unfair to us.
We are angry because He has been merciful to someone else.
And Jesus puts His finger directly on it:
“Do you begrudge my generosity?”
Matthew 20:15
That question can expose an entire lifetime of hidden spiritual pride.
Do you begrudge My generosity?
When the addict comes home?
When the adulterer genuinely repents?
When the prisoner bows before Christ?
When the person who mocked Christianity for thirty years suddenly calls Jesus Lord?
When somebody who squandered decades discovers the same Savior you have followed since childhood?
When the prodigal smells like pigs one morning and wears the father's robe by evening?
Do you rejoice?
Or somewhere underneath your religious vocabulary does something whisper...
“That isn't fair.”
Be careful.
Because that sentence may reveal that you have begun thinking of grace as wages.
Grace is not God finally paying good people what He owes them.
Grace is God rescuing sinners who could never place Him in their debt.
The Gospel destroys our spiritual résumé.
Scripture says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Not some.
All.
The respectable sinner.
The scandalous sinner.
The church-raised sinner.
The street-raised sinner.
The sinner holding a Bible.
The sinner holding a bottle.
The sinner whose rebellion became public.
And the sinner whose pride remained hidden beneath polished Christianity.
All have sinned.
That means there is only one reason anybody stands forgiven before a holy God.
Jesus Christ.
Not longevity.
Not reputation.
Not ministry activity.
Not theological vocabulary.
Not how many Christian posts you shared.
Not how many years you sat in church.
Not how clean your story looks beside somebody else's.
Christ.
His righteousness.
His cross.
His blood.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
That is why “the last will be first” can feel so offensive.
Jesus removes the measuring stick we secretly use to place ourselves above other people.
You may have entered the vineyard at sunrise.
Wonderful.
Serve Him faithfully.
Love Him deeply.
Finish well.
But never forget Who owns the vineyard.
The kingdom belongs to the King.
And His generosity is His to give.
This does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean sin is harmless.
It does not mean everyone automatically receives salvation regardless of their response to Christ.
Jesus did not die so that sin could be excused as insignificant.
He died because sin is so devastating that redemption required the cross.
Biblical grace does not say:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace says:
“Your sin mattered so much that the Son of God bore judgment for sinners—and His mercy is so astonishing that repentant sinners can be forgiven.”
That distinction changes everything.
Because perhaps you are reading this from the other side.
Maybe you are not the early worker.
Maybe you feel like the person arriving embarrassingly late.
Maybe you look backward and see wasted years.
A destroyed marriage.
An addiction.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Pride.
Greed.
An abortion you still cry about.
A child you abandoned.
A family you wounded.
A season where you wanted absolutely nothing to do with God.
Maybe you have spent so long believing you ruined your chance that you barely know how to pray anymore.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not announcing that your past was acceptable.
It is announcing something infinitely better:
Jesus Christ can redeem sinners.
The cross was not built for people who merely needed improvement.
Christ came to save.
There is still mercy at the feet of Jesus.
There is still forgiveness for the repentant.
There is still a robe for prodigals.
There is still restoration for failures.
There is still a Shepherd searching for sheep.
There is still blood powerful enough to cleanse.
You may have arrived late.
But if Christ is calling you...
come.
Do not stand outside the vineyard because you are ashamed that other people arrived earlier.
Come.
Do not wait until you feel worthy.
Come.
Do not attempt to clean yourself enough to deserve the invitation.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
The thief beside Jesus did not have decades left to build a Christian reputation.
He had nails.
A cross.
A criminal record.
A dying body.
And enough breath to turn toward Jesus.
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.”
He could not climb down and repair his reputation.
He could not spend twenty years proving that his conversion was authentic.
He could not build a ministry.
He could not give back everything he had taken.
He could not rewrite yesterday.
But beside him hung the One who could determine his tomorrow.
Jesus answered him:
“Today you will be with me in paradise.”
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace without a cross.
Grace purchased at an unimaginable price by Christ Himself.
And maybe that is exactly why this teaching makes us uncomfortable.
Because deep inside us is a little accountant.
It keeps records.
“I sacrificed more.”
“I obeyed longer.”
“I suffered more.”
“I served when nobody noticed.”
“I didn't do what they did.”
“I never walked away like that.”
“I stayed.”
And Jesus quietly asks:
Did you stay because you love Me...
or because you thought staying made Me owe you?
That question hurts.
Because religious pride can survive inside obedience.
A person can externally serve God while internally keeping score.
We can sing about amazing grace while secretly believing some people should receive less of it.
We can celebrate the prodigal son until God asks us to become the older brother standing outside the party deciding whether we can celebrate the father's mercy.
We want grace...
with rankings.
Jesus gives grace...
that leaves boasting outside.
Paul wrote:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith... not a result of works, so that no one may boast.”
Ephesians 2:8–9
No one may boast.
Not the person who arrived early.
Not the person who arrived late.
Not the preacher.
Not the former criminal.
Not the lifelong church member.
Not the rescued addict.
At the foot of the cross, human boasting suffocates.
There is only Christ.
And once you understand that, something beautiful begins happening.
You stop resenting testimonies that seem “too easy.”
You start celebrating when lost people come home.
You stop asking whether somebody deserves mercy.
You remember that mercy, by definition, is not something sinners earn.
You stop looking sideways at everyone else's portion.
You look upward at the Giver.
And suddenly the vineyard feels different.
You are no longer working to make the Master indebted to you.
You are working because the Master invited you in.
That is freedom.
Serve Jesus for fifty years if He gives you fifty years.
Serve Him for five if He gives you five.
Serve Him for five minutes if five minutes are all you have left.
But serve Him because He is worthy.
Not because you are negotiating wages with grace.
And if you have spent years running...
come home.
Today.
Not after you repair your reputation.
Not when Christians stop remembering what you did.
Not when your shame finally stops shouting.
Today.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Turn toward Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not the story of impressive people climbing toward God.
It is the story of a holy God coming down to rescue sinners.
Jesus lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He carried sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness and eternal life are found in Him.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by lowering God's holiness.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking guilty sinners and making them forgiven children of God through His redeeming work.
Maybe somebody reading this has been hiding.
If that is you, stop performing for one moment.
No polished testimony required.
Sometimes honesty is where healing conversations begin.
And Christian, there is another uncomfortable question.
Who came to your mind while reading this?
The person you almost subconsciously believed did not deserve another chance?
The family member who keeps running?
The friend buried beneath shame?
The believer who failed publicly?
The person who thinks Christianity could never possibly want somebody like them?
Send this article to them.
They need to know the cross still stands.
They need to know repentance is still possible.
They need to know grace is not permission to remain in darkness; it is Christ calling sinners out of darkness and into life.
Because eventually you may become the early worker again.
Eventually you may watch God bless, restore, forgive, or use somebody whose history bothers you.
When that day comes, come back and remember:
The vineyard belongs to Him.
The grace belongs to Him.
The glory belongs to Him.
It does not.
Not because financial support earns spiritual merit.
It cannot.
And never because anyone can buy grace.
Grace was purchased by Christ, not by us.
But one practical way believers can glorify God is by willingly using the resources He has entrusted to them to help Gospel-centered ministry continue reaching people.
Not merely for reach.
For the person behind the reach.
The exhausted believer.
The ashamed prodigal.
The secret sinner.
The skeptical friend.
The person sitting in darkness at two in the morning convinced God would never want them.
Maybe your share becomes the doorway through which they hear one sentence they desperately needed:
You are not saved because you arrived first.
You are saved by Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the deepest reason “the last will be first” makes us uncomfortable.
It destroys our rankings.
It dismantles our boasting.
It confronts our envy.
It exposes our scorekeeping.
Then it leaves us standing beside everyone else who needs mercy...
looking toward the same crucified and risen Savior.
So when another sinner comes stumbling home...
do not complain that the Father opened the door.
Celebrate.
Because if grace were only given to people who deserved it...
the house would be empty.
Remember this when your past accuses you, and remember it when somebody else's past tempts you to accuse them:
At the cross, nobody gets to brag about arriving first—only to marvel that Jesus opened the door at all.
